desc:
Start with the empty string. In one step you may insert the three-letter block 'abc' at any position of the current string, including in the middle of an earlier block. Given a string s, return true if some sequence of such steps produces exactly s, and false otherwise.

Examples: 'aabcbc' is possible (insert abc into the middle of abc), and so is 'abcabcababcc'. The string 'abccba' is not.
constraints: s consists only of the letters a, b and c
hints: Think backwards: the last inserted block must appear in s as a contiguous 'abc'. Remove it and the rest must again be buildable.
Removing blocks one by one with replace is slow if repeated. Which occurrence of 'abc' do you discover first when reading left to right?
Scan with a stack: push every character, and whenever the top three characters are a, b, c, pop them. The string is buildable exactly when the stack ends up empty.
editorial: Reverse the process. If s was produced by insertions, then the most recently inserted block is a contiguous 'abc' inside s; deleting it leaves a string that was produced by one step less. So s is buildable if and only if repeatedly deleting an 'abc' substring can reduce it to the empty string. The order of deletions does not matter, because two occurrences of 'abc' can never overlap.

Do the deletions with a stack: push characters one by one and, whenever the three topmost characters spell abc, pop them. The stack holds exactly the reduced text of the prefix read so far. If it is empty at the end, the answer is true. A quick shortcut is that the length must be divisible by 3. Time O(n), space O(n).
